sections.body:
Emotional maturity is the capacity to stay in charge of your own reactions when the other person is difficult. It is not calmness, and it is not the absence of strong feeling. It is what happens between the feeling and the act: how long the gap is, and whether your act leaves the situation better or worse.

The word is used loosely, so this article works with a definition made of five parts. You can look for all five in a colleague, and you can check all five in yourself.

Self-regulation is the pause between the feeling and the act: the moment where you could have reacted and did not. **Empathy** is reading what the other person feels and taking it seriously enough to act on it. **Accountability** is owning the effect of your behaviour and repairing what it broke. **Tolerance of frustration** is staying with a delay, a refusal or a mistake instead of making the other person pay for it. **Clarity** is saying what you feel and what you need, accurately, without turning it into a charge.

Two limits belong to the definition. Maturity is not the same as being pleasant: a person can be fair, clear and firm and still say no to you. And it is not a state you reach once; it is a set of habits that cost more on a bad day than on a good one. How much of it can be taught, and how much comes from temperament and from the family you grew up in, is still argued over. Nothing here depends on the answer: whatever the split, the five parts are behaviour you can see, and behaviour you can see is the only part two people can talk about.
examples: Emotional maturity is the pause, not the calm voice.
He could have walked out, and he did not; that pause was his self-regulation.
Her empathy showed in the question she asked instead of the advice she gave.
His accountability was naming what he had broken before anyone asked.
sections.heading: What emotional maturity is, and the five parts of it

terms.example: Her emotional maturity showed in the pause before she answered, not in the answer itself.
terms.gloss: The capacity to stay in charge of your own reactions when the other person is difficult.

terms.example: He used self-regulation to stay in the room instead of walking out.
terms.gloss: The capacity to hold a reaction and choose when to act on it.

terms.example: Her empathy showed in the question she asked instead of the advice she gave.
terms.gloss: Reading what another person feels, and taking it seriously enough to act on it.

terms.example: Accountability came first: he named what he had broken and what he would do about it.
terms.gloss: Owning the effect of your behaviour and repairing what it damaged.

terms.example: Tolerance of frustration is what a good team leader buys with a calm answer on a Friday.
terms.gloss: The capacity to stay with a delay, a refusal or a mistake without making the other person pay for it.

sections.body:
Most of the vocabulary of this subject describes a behaviour you can watch, not a quality you can admire. A **trait** is a stable leaning — a disposition that shows up across situations and across time. A **behaviour** is one act, in one moment, with one person in front of you. The words below point at behaviours, because a behaviour is the part two people can ask about, agree on and change.

Three words describe how you hold your own reaction. **Self-regulation** is the process of holding a reaction and choosing when to act on it; the same idea is often called *emotional regulation*. **Impulsivity** is the opposite leaning: acting first and looking afterwards. **Stress reactivity** is how fast and how hard you react to pressure — a tempo rather than a character. A person with a fast tempo is not immature, and the same person can have excellent self-regulation on a calm day and none at all on the day the line is down.

One word names the work that nobody puts on a report. **Emotional labour** is the effort of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the situation keeps running: the tone you set, the mood you repair, the face you keep when you would rather not. It is not a personality trait. It is a job, and somebody is doing it in every team and every household — often without being asked and often without being thanked.

And one word is the popular name for the whole subject: **emotional intelligence**. It is used at work for a set of skills that overlap with the ones described here. Researchers disagree about how well it can be measured, and in a meeting the label is often used to dismiss a colleague instead of describing one. Use it to name a skill; do not use it as a verdict.
examples: His impulsivity was a tempo, not a character: the same man was steady in the morning and not at midnight.
Emotional labour is a job, and somebody in the room is doing it.
Emotional intelligence is a label people use loosely; ask which skill they mean.
A trait is a leaning; a behaviour is what you can ask about.
sections.heading: The words of the subject, and what they point at

terms.example: The message went out in impatience, and the impulsivity cost him the job.
terms.gloss: The leaning towards acting before you have looked at what the act will do.

terms.example: Her stress reactivity is high in meetings and low in front of a machine.
terms.gloss: How strongly and how fast a person reacts to pressure; a tempo, not a character.

terms.example: Emotional labour is the invisible work of keeping a meeting calm.
terms.gloss: The work of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the situation keeps running.

sections.body:
Every word of this subject has a professional voice and a private one, and they are not the same sentence. At work the sentence is softened so that the point survives. At home it is plain. Both are correct, and using the wrong one in the wrong place is how a fair point becomes a fight.

Affective empathy and **cognitive empathy** separate cleanly in both places. In a meeting, the professional sentence is about the situation: *Can you tell me what you saw from your side?* — that is cognitive empathy, the angle. The private sentence is about the feeling: *You looked shaken, and I did not notice until now.* — that is affective empathy, the mirror. A person can do the first and not the second, and the second is what tells the other person they were seen.

Assertiveness is blunt in both registers, and the difference is in the aim. At work: *I need the report by Friday, and I need two hours to write it.* At home: *I want to say this without it turning into a fight, so I am going to say it slowly.* The first asks for a thing. The second asks for a chance, and it gets one.

Conflict avoidance sounds like a virtue at work and can be a wall in a relationship. The professional sentence is *Let us take it offline; I do not want to hold the room.* The private sentence is *I did not want to say it here, so now we are saying it here.* In both, the same thing happens: the disagreement is postponed, and a postponed disagreement keeps its interest.
examples: Can you tell me what you saw from your side?
I need the report by Friday, and I need two hours to write it.
You looked shaken, and I did not notice until now.
Let us take it offline; I do not want to hold the room.
sections.heading: The same words at work and at home

terms.example: Affective empathy made her notice that the new engineer was frightened in the group.
terms.gloss: The feeling part of empathy: catching what the other person feels.

terms.example: Cognitive empathy is what lets you guess that the deadline was the real problem.
terms.gloss: The thinking part of empathy: seeing the situation from the other person's side.

terms.example: Assertiveness is saying the report is late and then saying what you need instead.
terms.gloss: Stating your need, your limit or your disagreement without wrapping it in blame.

terms.example: Conflict avoidance kept the meeting pleasant and the problem on the table.
terms.gloss: The leaning that keeps the peace by not raising the issue at all.

sections.body:
A claim about two groups is a claim about two centres. The honest sentence is narrow: *on this measure, in this sample, the average of one group is higher than the average of the other.* Everything goes wrong when that sentence is stretched onto a person: *women are more emotional*, *men cannot handle feelings*, *men and women think differently*. The stretch happens silently, and the stretched sentence is the one people then argue about.

The reason is arithmetic, and it is worth seeing plainly. A group is not one value; it is a spread of values. The average is one point inside that spread, and the point says nothing about how wide the spread is. Put two spreads side by side and their centres can be measurably apart while the two shapes still overlap so much that most members of one group fall inside the range of the other. That **overlap** is the part that matters for the person standing in front of you; the distance between the centres is the part that matters for the study.

So a claim about a group cannot tell you about an individual, even when the claim is perfectly true. People inside one group are spread out from end to end, and the two ends of the same group have little in common with each other. Two things make this harder in practice. The first is the difference between what a person shows and what a person feels: keeping a reaction off your face so that the room does not have to deal with it is something people learn, and different groups learn different rules of display, so a difference in expression is not a difference in feeling. The second is the role people play: a result collected in one workplace, one age group or one culture does not travel to another, because the roles people occupy change how they behave.

The last step is the **stereotype**: a belief about a group applied to a person without looking at that person. Every stereotype starts as an average somebody heard and repeated, and the repetition is where the error enters — the measure is forgotten, then the sample, then the culture, then the situation, until what is left is a rule about people. The research on this subject is not settled, and this article does not pretend that it is. Some studies report average differences between men and women on measures of empathy, on impulse control and on the display of emotion; other studies report differences that are small, or that change with the measure or the context. The argument is about the result and about the method at the same time: which instrument, which sample, which age, which words on the questionnaire. Two answers are on the table. One says the differences are real but small and heavily overlapping, so they are a weak prior and never a rule. The other says much of what looks like a difference is produced by how the question was asked and who was asked. Follow either answer and the instruction is the same: judge the person in front of you by what they do, and hold a claim about a group as the start of a question.
examples: On this measure, in this sample, the average of one group is higher than the average of the other.
The two averages are apart, but the overlap is wide, so the average says little about the person in front of me.
That is a stereotype: a claim about a group applied to a person I have not looked at.
A difference in what people show is not a difference in what they feel.
sections.heading: What a claim about an average can and cannot tell you

terms.example: That sentence about men and women is a stereotype, and it settles nothing about the man in front of you.
terms.gloss: A belief about a group that is applied to a person without looking at that person.

terms.example: The overlap between the two groups is wide, so the average says very little about one person.
terms.gloss: The part of the value ranges of two groups that lies on top of each other.

sections.body:
Claims about differences between groups are easy to repeat and hard to check, because the sentence that travels is always shorter than the sentence that was measured. The table is a reading procedure. For each kind of claim it says what the claim supports, what it does not support, and the one question that decides whether you can use it.

The questions in the last column are short on purpose. If nobody can answer one of them, the claim is not ready for a decision, a meeting or an argument — not because it is false, but because nobody has said what it rests on.

Read every row with the **overlap** in mind. A claim that survives the question in its last column is still a claim about a group, and it still says nothing about the person in front of you.
examples: On this measure, in this sample — that is how far the claim goes.
Small compared with what? Small next to the spread inside each group is a different statement.
Which measure, and how was it measured?
sections.heading: How to read a claim before you use it

headers: The question to ask before you use it
rows: On this measure, in this sample, the average of one group is higher than the average of the other.
A difference of averages in the sample that was studied.
Any statement about a person from either group.
How wide is the spread inside each group, and how much do the two spreads overlap?
Men and women differ in average emotional maturity.
That the two averages differ on the measure that was used.
A rule about any man or any woman.
Which measure of emotional maturity, and how was it measured?
Women are more empathetic than men.
A difference on the empathy measure that was used.
That a woman will understand you better, or that a man will not.
Affective empathy or cognitive empathy, and does the measure predict behaviour in a real conversation?
Men show less emotion than women.
That the participants behaved differently in front of the person who recorded them.
That the men felt less.
Was the difference in the feeling, or in what the participants were willing to show?
The difference is small.
That the two centres are close together.
That the two groups are the same.
Small compared with what: the spread inside each group?
The difference is caused by hormones, by genes, or by culture.
A proposed mechanism that can be tested.
That the mechanism has been proved.
What would separate this explanation from the other two?

sections.body:
Six steps. They work with a partner, with a colleague and with a family member, and they take one conversation, not a campaign. The steps do not settle the question of which group is more mature; they settle the question of what you are going to ask for today.

The first two steps remove the group from the room. A claim about men and women in the middle of a conversation about one behaviour is an escalation: it turns one person into a side, and it asks the other person to defend a side they never chose. Name the behaviour and ask what the other person meant, and the conversation stays on something that can change.

The last two steps are about what happens after the sentence. Say the need instead of the accusation, so that the other person has something to answer. Then agree on one small thing you can both check, and put the date in the note. A conversation with no next step turns into a memory, and a memory is won by whoever repeats it loudest.
examples: In the last three meetings you answered over me twice, and I lost the thread of my own report.
What did you need at that moment?
I need ten minutes, and I need to finish my sentence.
Let us leave the general question aside and stay with the meeting.
sections.heading: How to have the conversation without a fight
steps: Name the behaviour, not the group: say what happened, when, and what it did to you, and leave the category out of it.
Ask what the other person meant before you explain your reading of it; the answer is often a need you did not know about.
Say the need instead of the accusation: instead of 'you never listen', say 'I need ten minutes and I need to finish my sentence'.
Move the argument out of the group: if the conversation turns to men and women in general, park it for later and come back to the behaviour in front of you.
Agree on one thing to try, small enough to check: one change, one owner, one date.
Write the agreement down and set the moment you will look at it again, because a conversation with no next date becomes a memory.

sections.body:
This article does not settle the debate. It does not tell you whether men or women are more emotionally mature, because that question is not settled in the research, and an article that answered it would be making up the answer. It does not rank the two groups for you either. The honest position is that the average difference, where it exists, is smaller than the spread inside each group, and the practical instruction does not change whichever way the research moves.

It does not measure anybody. There is no test you can run on your partner, your colleague or yourself that produces a maturity score, and a questionnaire sold as one is not a measurement of you. What you can do is watch the five parts in one specific moment, and say what you saw.

And it does not excuse a behaviour because it is common. If many people of any group interrupt, or withdraw, or lie about their feelings, the behaviour is still a choice that each person makes, and the people who are near it still pay for it. Knowing the vocabulary of this argument does not make you right in it either: a person who can list the six steps is still able to interrupt.
examples: This article does not settle the debate, and I am not going to pretend that it does.
There is no maturity score, and a questionnaire that gives you one is not measuring you.
A pattern can be common and still be a choice, and the people near it still pay for it.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
Use these when the moment arrives, not afterwards. The first two are for a partner, the next two for a colleague, the next two for a family, and the last two for writing. None of them needs a dramatic voice, and none of them needs the word always.

The point of every one of them is the same: the behaviour is named, the need is stated, and the other person has something to answer. That is what keeps a conversation about a difference from turning into a fight about a group.
examples: You went quiet for three days after we talked about money, and I did not know what to do with that.
I am not angry at you. I am tired, and I need ten minutes before I can talk about it properly.
In yesterday's review you answered over me twice, and I lost my own point.
Can you tell me what you saw from your side? I may have missed something.
You do this every time we talk about my sister, and I would like to talk about it when nobody is upset.
I know this is a hard day for you, and I still need the report on my desk by Friday.
Thank you for sending this. One question before I approve it: who has the spare part?
To be clear about what I need: two hours with the file, and no interruptions between 14:00 and 16:00.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: An average difference between two groups says where the centres of two clouds sit, not where any one person stands. After reading this you can name the five parts of emotional maturity, say what a claim about men and women can and cannot tell you about one person, read a group claim without turning it into a rule, and hold a conversation about it without the argument becoming a fight.
item.title: Gender Differences in Emotional Maturity
